What replaced them at the centre of Mediterranean exchange was a set of merchant cities with no empire and no great king, which is the chapter's lesson about coupling, restated from the other side.^[**Sources:** Cline, *After 1177 B.C.: The Survival of Civilizations* (2021), ch. 3, "The Mediterranean Became a Phoenician Lake", for the continuity of the Canaanite population, the anti-fragile reading of Phoenicia and Cyprus, and the Carol Bell quotation; Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire, 550-202 BCE*, on the Levantine cities after the collapse. Cited by chapter: the held edition is an EPUB without pagination. **Read more:** Cline (2021).] One document shows the change better than any argument about it. Around 1075 BCE an Egyptian temple official named Wenamun was sent from Karnak to Byblos to buy cedar for a ceremonial barge. In the Amarna world of two centuries earlier this would have been a matter between courts. It was not any more. Wenamun was robbed at Dor on the way; the prince of Byblos, Tjekkerbaal, received him with open hostility; and the timber was not cut until payment had been shipped from Egypt and inspected. The payment is itemised, and reads like an invoice: four gold bowls and another gold vessel, five bowls of silver, ten pieces of clothing, five hundred mats of smooth linen, five hundred ox hides, five hundred ropes, twenty sacks of lentils and five baskets of fish.

Only then did the prince detail three hundred men and three hundred oxen to fell the trees, which lay through the winter before being hauled to the shore. An Egyptian priest could no longer requisition Lebanese cedar on the strength of who he served. He had to buy it, in advance, from a man who was free to be rude to him. That is the shift from the gift economy the Uluburun ship was carrying to a price economy, recorded in one bad-tempered voyage.^[**Sources:** Cline, *After 1177 B.C.* (2021), ch. 3, quoting and discussing the Tale of Wenamun, with the itemised payment and the felling of the timber; the voyage is dated to about 1075 BCE. The Tale is a literary text of uncertain historicity, and should be taught as a story that reflects commercial conditions rather than as a transaction record. **Read more:** Cline (2021), ch. 3.] The most famous thing they made was a colour, and it is perhaps the clearest illustration the ancient world offers of a price set by scarce supply meeting status-driven demand rather than by the cost of the raw material. Purple dye comes from a gland that has to be cut from a living sea snail, with the shell broken to reach it, which is why the archaeological signature of a dye-works is a bed of crushed shells rather than whole ones. The quantities are brutal: experimental archaeology puts about two hundred snails into a square of wool 125 centimetres on a side to reach a deep purple, and at least five thousand into a whole cloak, while older estimates ran to twenty thousand animals for a garment's trim alone. A batch took four days at minimum, and the work stank badly enough that Strabo, centuries later, thought it made Tyre unpleasant to live in. It would be wrong to conclude that the labour made the value, because if effort made things valuable every laborious process would be lucrative.

What made purple dear was that an inelastic, labour-bound supply met courts that would pay almost anything for a colour only they were permitted to wear. States knew exactly where that left them. In a Hittite letter of the early thirteenth century a vassal complains that a raid has cost him his purple-dyers --- three groups of them, one his own, one the king's, one belonging to a god --- and the diplomatic effort to recover them is the substance of the letter. Skilled dyers were capital, and were treated as such.^[**Sources:** Silver, *The Purpled World* (2023), reporting Ruscillo's experimental work on murex yields and the Hittite correspondence on captured dyers. Note that the held copy of Silver lacks book pagination, so these are cited by section; the underlying experimental figures are Ruscillo (2005). Silver also reads the Aegean Bronze Age textile and purple trade as evidence of a far more commercialised world than the orthodox picture allows, even casting the Trojan War as a trade war; that bolder reading is a contested hypothesis rather than settled fact. **Read more:** Silver (2023).]

![*Bolinus brandaris*, the murex sea-snail from which Tyrian purple was won at enormous labour --- a processed luxury whose value lay in the work locked into it. Photo: H. Zell, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.](book/figures/photos/murex.jpg){#fig-murex width=52%}

From the tenth century these cities founded settlements westward --- Cyprus first, then North Africa, Sardinia and Sicily, and by about 800 to 780 BCE, on radiocarbon dates, southern Spain --- and among them was *Qart Hadasht*, New City, which is Carthage. The traditional foundation date of 814 BCE is a Greek chronographer's arithmetic rather than an excavated one; the archaeology says late ninth or early eighth century and declines to say more. Carthage was nobody yet: through this chapter's period it was a modest, peripheral, largely mud-brick town, one of the least archaeologically visible of the western foundations, and the empire it later built belongs to the next chapter. What drove them west is the interesting question, and it is genuinely open. The traditional answer is metals. Silver was becoming a proto-currency across the Iron Age Near East, with thirty-four silver hoards recovered from Cisjordan alone, and demand for it was sharpened by three things at once: the collapse of the Bronze Age exchange networks, the Levant's own lack of silver, and the rise of the Neo-Assyrian empire with its appetite for tribute. On this reading, first argued at length by Susan Frankenstein and developed by Maria Eugenia Aubet, the western settlements were commercial factories and the whole diaspora was a response to Assyrian pressure on Tyre, and the mining frontiers do open when the model predicts, in south-western Spain and at Laurion in the Aegean.

The case against is archaeological, and it is not that the metals trade did not happen but that it does not explain the settlements, since the excavated colonies look like farms, agricultural towns from their foundation. [Appendix E](appendix-e-disputes.qmd) sets out the argument. This chapter takes the position the evidence supports and no more: the metals demand was real, the settlements were more than trading posts, and the westward silver flow that the tidiest version of the story wants remains an inference rather than a demonstrated fact.^[**Sources:** Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire*, on the western foundation sequence, the radiocarbon dating of the Iberian settlements, the status of the 814 BCE tradition, Carthage's archaeological invisibility before about 650 BCE, and at p. 61 for the negative case and for the Huelva sherd counts, sailing distances and agricultural character of the settlements; López-Ruiz and Doak (eds), *The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean* (2019), for the Iron Age silver economy and the Cisjordan hoards, for the Frankenstein thesis and Aubet's commercial-diaspora development of it, and for the shift away from exclusively commercial explanations of colonization. **Read more:** López-Ruiz and Doak (2019).] A word about the people already there, because this section has so far been told from the ships. The society the Phoenicians met in south-western Iberia is known as Tartessos, and the temptation is to file it as the native partner in a colonial encounter. Sebastián Celestino and Carolina López-Ruiz argue that this gets the thing backwards. Tartessos, on their account, cannot be understood as an impermeable entity separate from the contact: it *is* the cultural horizon that the contact produced, formed from an indigenous substratum meeting several waves of Phoenician settlement, with contributions from elsewhere in the Mediterranean at different stages. There was no fixed Tartessian culture that the Phoenicians then traded with; the two made a third thing together. It is also, they note, a society known almost entirely through other people's writing, having left no historical narrative of its own, which is the same evidential predicament as the Phoenicians themselves and a reason to be careful about who gets described as the active party.^[**Sources:** Celestino Pérez and López-Ruiz, *Tartessos and the Phoenicians in Iberia* (Oxford University Press), for the argument that Tartessos is the product of contact rather than a pre-existing entity encountered by it, and for the absence of self-generated written narratives. **Read more:** Celestino Pérez and López-Ruiz.]

Two other things travelled with the pots, and the first was a script. Short Phoenician inscriptions, mostly personal names and ownership marks, turn up scratched on ordinary locally made jars in the harbour houses of Castillo de Dona Blanca near Gadir --- thirty-eight of them from the eighth and seventh centuries --- and by the seventh century the Iberians around Gadir were writing too, on objects of trade. This is writing as a merchant's tool rather than a bureaucracy's, and it is the counter-case to Uruk. Cuneiform was expensive: it took hundreds of signs, a scribal career to learn them, and it grew out of running a large institution's accounts. The Phoenician script was a consonantal alphabet of twenty-two letters, one for each consonantal phoneme in the language, and a trader could carry it in his head. A consonantal alphabet had been adapted to the cuneiform technique at Ugarit in the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BCE, but the schematised, reduced form that became the Phoenician script came into common use around the twelfth century or a little later, in the specialists' own phrasing with the reopening of trade links after the collapse.

From there it went everywhere: to the Israelites, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites and Aramaeans, whose national scripts are all essentially its children; westward with the settlements; and into the Aegean, where the Greeks adapted it, adding vowels, with the oldest Greek alphabetic inscriptions dating to about the second quarter of the eighth century BCE. The economic point is the one to carry forward. When the cost of learning to record a transaction falls from a career to an afternoon, record-keeping stops being a function of the state. Uruk's accounting produced a scribal class; Tyre's produced a merchant class that could write. Both are answers to the same problem, and the second is very much cheaper.^[**Sources:** López-Ruiz and Doak (eds), *The Oxford Handbook of the Phoenician and Punic Mediterranean* (2019), on the twenty-two-letter consonantal alphabet and its match to Phoenician phonology, the Ugaritic cuneiform antecedent, the schematised script emerging around the twelfth century with the reopening of trade links, its spread through the Levantine national scripts, and the dating of the Greek adaptation by grapheme comparison; Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire*, on the Castillo de Dona Blanca inscriptions and indigenous Iberian writing at Gadir. The claim that the script's cheapness had economic consequences is this book's inference from those facts, not a finding the handbook states. **Read more:** López-Ruiz and Doak (2019).] The other thing that travelled was competition. Within two centuries the neighbours had learned the writing, the farming and the politics, and Greek settlement in the western Mediterranean came to outnumber Phoenician. Settler counts measure presence rather than commercial advantage, so read that as a sign and not a measurement; but what it points at, advantage decaying by imitation once the technique is cheap to copy, is a pattern this book will meet again in Venice, in Amsterdam and in Lancashire. By 500 BCE the pieces of the next order were in place. Persia had reunited the Near East, iron had loosened the tin bottleneck, the Lydians had struck the first coins and the Greeks were already minting small change, and Carthage, still a modest city, had founded its own first colony, Ebusus, in 654 BCE. The board was reset.^[**Sources:** Pilkington, *The Carthaginian Empire*, on the relative numbers of Greek and Phoenician settlers by 600 BCE and on Ebusus. **Note on a gap:** the held corpus supports the archaeology of merchant literacy but not the history of the alphabet itself --- its letter count, its date, or the mechanism of its transmission to Greek. **Read more:** Pilkington.]

## Reading the period: the four questions

The three thousand years from about 3500 to 500 BCE can be put through the same four questions that drive the rest of this book, with the warning that the answers here are softer than any later chapter's, because the evidence is thinner and the system looser. They are worth running all the same, because this is where the questions themselves are forged. The first question was about direction, and the answer is that the system did both, repeatedly, with no single arc running through the period. The three cycles narrated above --- the Uruk sphere, the Gulf trade, the Late Bronze Age palace economies --- each integrated and then came apart, which is the module's rhythm in miniature. The lesson the sequence bequeathed to every later chapter is that integration bred fragility: the routes that carried trade also carried shocks, and a more connected system was a more exposed one. The Collapse of 1177 BCE is the clearest instance in the book, because the palace economies that failed together were the most tightly coupled thing the ancient world had built.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 1199); Kriwaczek (Page 72); Cline (Loc 507). **Read more:** Cline, *1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed* (2014).]

The second question was about channels, and this period's answer is that all three of the module's corridors were born here at once: the maritime Indian Ocean, the desert and oasis route that would later be called the Silk Road, and the great Eurasian steppe. Of the three, the steppe was the era's dynamic engine rather than its periphery, a band of unbroken grass running some seven thousand kilometres from eastern Europe to the Great Wall of China. The ocean, the corridor this book centres on, was still largely waiting, its monsoon geography laid down but its traffic thin. To see how the channels actually worked it helps to follow one good, and the most revealing is tin. Bronze, the period's defining metal, needed it, yet tin lay almost nowhere near the cities that used it, so it had to travel long distances to reach them --- and its price marked the route, in barter ratios that the cuneiform records preserve centuries before any coin existed to express them. The volumes were not trivial either: a single cargo such as the one lost off Uluburun around 1300 BCE carried perhaps a tonne of tin in one hull.^[**Sources:** Cunliffe (Loc 158, 909); Frahm (Page 47); Anthony (Loc 6829); Cline (Loc 1646). **Read more:** Cunliffe, *By Steppe, Desert, and Ocean* (2015).]

::: {.callout-important}
## Follow the money
With no coins yet, the period's bullion tracer was the relative price of metals, and tin is the clearest one to track. It had to travel because bronze needed it and it lay far from the cities that consumed it. The gap between its price at Assur, about 6.7 shekels of silver per 100 shekels of tin, and in Anatolia, about 14.3, moved the metal from where it was cheap toward where it was dear, centuries before coinage. The gap is also a measurement: roughly a doubling over 950 kilometres is what carriage cost in this technology, and later chapters watch that wedge narrow. On the [Introduction](00-introduction.qmd)'s test --- a gap bounded by the cost of carriage --- that makes Assur and Kanesh about as integrated as the technology of the day allowed, and the measure of later integration is not that such gaps disappear but that they shrink toward the physical cost of carriage. This is the same "follow the metal" logic the module will use for millennia to locate the centre, except that here it shows up in barter ratios scratched onto clay rather than in the output of any mint.
:::

![The price of distance: 100 shekels of tin cost about 6.7 shekels of silver at Assur but about 14.3 in Anatolia, where it was scarcer. The gap is not arbitrage --- it is the cost of carriage, quoted, centuries before any coin existed to express it, and integration is that wedge narrowing (stylised; values from the Old Assyrian records). Source: Frahm.](book/figures/tin-arbitrage-01.png){#fig-tin width=72%}

![A single Bronze Age cargo as a dataset of one: the Uluburun wreck (c.1300 BCE) carried ~10 tonnes of copper and ~1 tonne of tin --- the ~10:1 bronze recipe --- plus glass, resin, ivory and amber, with products of at least nine or ten cultures. Bulk metal moved by sea long before coins (estimated tonnages). Source: Cline.](book/figures/uluburun-cargo-01.png){#fig-uluburun width=66%}

The third question was about modes: what crossed the connection? Two kinds of thing did, and the chapter is clearer if they are kept apart. On one side are real flows, and the production function names them: output itself moves as goods, useful knowledge as technique, people as labour, produced assets as capital. On the other side run monetary and financial flows, things that settle a transaction and claims that carry purchasing power across time. Silver sits on both sides at once, which is the complication this period is best at teaching. The evidence for each is a different instrument. Goods are somebody else's land, arriving in usable form. A cargo of tin is a mineral endowment that Mesopotamia did not have, and that is what makes tin and not grain the story: a small flow of an input nothing can substitute for has more structural consequence than a large flow of something anybody can grow. High-value processed goods travelled too, and mattered out of proportion to their bulk, because a supply that could not easily be expanded met a demand that would pay almost anything --- Ugarit paid its yearly tribute to the Hittites not only in gold but in dyed wool and finished garments, cloth being among the most concentrated stores of value a Bronze Age economy could ship, and the Tyrian purple described above is the vivid later case.

There is also one piece of evidence here for the other side of the equation, and the archaeology of trade almost never reaches it: demand. Ancient proteins recovered from dental calculus at Bronze Age Megiddo, around 1650 to 1320 BCE, record what individual people actually put in their mouths --- cereals, sesame and dates as expected, and then soybean in one individual, turmeric in one, probable banana in one. At least one person in the second-millennium Levant ate a South Asian spice and a South Asian pulse. What that licenses is narrow. It establishes contact and is silent on commerce; it cannot say how many, how often, or whether a market existed, and every exotic in the study rests on a single person. The study's authors read it less cautiously than this and write of a pattern of established trade, and the gap between what evidence licenses and what is claimed from it, including by the people who produced it, is worth more to an economist than the finding.^[**Sources:** Scott et al. (2021) on the Megiddo and Tel Erani dental calculus; the identifications rest on two and three peptides respectively, at or barely above the standard authentication threshold; Cline (Loc 2308) on Ugarit's tribute in cloth. **Note:** there is no published rebuttal of these identifications --- the caution here is this book's reading of a general methodological standard, not a critique in the literature. **Read more:** Scott et al., "Exotic foods reveal contact between South Asia and the Near East", *PNAS* 118 (2021).]

Technology moved, and it moved slowly. The chariot took something like eight hundred years to cross a continent, from Sintashta graves east of the Urals before 2000 BCE to China around 1200, and that is the diffusion speed of this world. People moved, and two studies measure it in a way no document can. The Harappan cemeteries are the first. Strontium and lead isotopes in tooth enamel, seventy-seven teeth from fifty-five individuals at Harappa and Farmana, and the design is what makes the result strong: the three molars form at different ages, so one skeleton yields an ordered sequence of childhood residences rather than an average. First molars fall outside the local range; second and third converge on it, at Farmana around three to five years of age. These were first-generation immigrants. The economics is in where they came from. The migrants point north-west to the upper Indus and north-east to the Punjab plains, and the lead in the Farmana burials points at the Khetri copper belt about a hundred and fifty kilometres south, so migrants and metals travelled the same corridors. Resource peripheries exported the material and the people who knew how to get it, which is a relationship this chapter meets again at its far end, in Cornwall.

The sample will not carry a migration rate, and the reason is a selection rule rather than a small sample size: fewer than six hundred Indus skeletons exist from a century of excavation across some 680,000 square kilometres, and formal cemetery burial is rare within that. A cemetery here is a complete sample of a small institution rather than a thin random sample of Indus society.^[**Sources:** Valentine et al. (2015) on strontium and lead isotopes at Harappa and Farmana. **Caveats the authors state:** the local range is defined from faunal samples whose spread suggests some of the animals were themselves imported, which makes the non-local verdict conservative but is an inference; breastfeeding by immigrant mothers and childhood exposure to imported lead-bearing cosmetics are argued against rather than eliminated; the South Asian ore and slag reference data are in the authors' own word equivocal. **Read more:** Valentine et al., *PLOS ONE* 10 (2015).] The second study is in Britain, and it measures a flow of people with no price attached to it at all. Five isotope systems run on 131 pigs from four Late Neolithic henge complexes in southern Britain, around 2800 to 2400 BCE, and the strontium range at Durrington Walls is wider than at any other published British site, wider than a Roman legionary fortress sitting on far more varied geology, while three kilometres away Middle Neolithic animals from West Amesbury Farm show the narrowest range of any British assemblage. So the wide catchment is not a property of the landscape; it is new, and it is institutional. The economics turns on the animal, because pigs drive badly over distance and there is no reason to walk one for hundreds of kilometres rather than carry the meat, unless the animal and the people who raised it are meant to arrive together. The isotopes are therefore measuring the geographic reach of a mobilisation organised without money, writing, prices or a market. Hold it in mind for the fourth question: peripheral in a network is not the same thing as simple.^[**Sources:** Madgwick et al. (2019), the largest fully published multi-isotope faunal dataset in archaeology. **Caveat:** provenance here is by exclusion --- the animals are shown not to be local, not traced to farms --- and with thin British comparative data for sulfur and oxygen, most of the geographic weight rests on strontium. **Read more:** Madgwick et al., *Science Advances* 5 (2019).]

Capital was present and thin. Ships, pack animals, irrigation works, workshops and stores are the capital of this world, and there is nothing in it that could be called a capital market. That point needs care, because finance in this period was sophisticated without being broad, and the two are easy to confuse. Money and credit are not capital; they are what let capital be assembled and what bridges the delay between committing resources and getting them back. That delay is the thing to picture: perhaps a hundred days between committing goods at Assur and seeing any silver return, with the donkeys, fodder, drivers and tolls all paid for in advance. A trade with that shape cannot run on cash in hand. So it ran on credit, and we know it did because the Kanesh archive is a merchant archive: some twelve thousand private letters and account tablets from the trading families themselves rather than from a palace.

For once in this period we are reading the traders, and the claims and obligations in those letters are denominated in silver, across households and across a political frontier, with no coin anywhere in the system. The institutional depth goes back further. Interest-bearing debt is securely attested from the later third millennium and may reach to about 3000 BCE, and rulers periodically wiped the slate: the earliest recorded is Enmetena of Lagash, around 2400 BCE, and the Sumerian word for what he granted was *amargi*, literally a return to the mother, debtors going home. It is the earliest attested word for freedom in any written language, and the first freedom in the written record is freedom from debt.

One last flow belongs here, and it complicates this book's own spine before the spine has started. Before coinage, silver in the Levant circulated as hacksilver, cut and weighed, and because it was not endlessly remelted its lead-isotope signature reads onto the ore field that was worked. Seventy-five items from three dated Phoenician hoards show the source moving: Anatolian silver is prominent in the tenth and ninth centuries, but by the ninth-century hoard at Ein Hofez only two of twenty-nine items are consistent with Anatolian ore and most point to Iberia. The metal is running west to east. The expectation set up by [Chapter 5](05-world-becomes-one.qmd) and [Chapter 6](06-companies-coercion.qmd) is that silver flows toward Asia. The first traceable flow in the record does the opposite. Direction is a function of where the ore sits and where the demand sits, and both of those move.^[**Sources:** Eshel et al. (2019) on lead isotopes in hacksilver from Dor, Akko and Ein Hofez; Frahm (Page 47) and Goetzmann (loc 592, 836) on Old Assyrian credit; Graeber (Loc 8075, 4560) on the *amargi* cancellations; Barjamovic, Chaney, Cosar and Hortacsu (2019), *QJE* 134(3), on the Kanesh corpus. **Caveats:** many hacksilver items are mixtures rather than single-source, and copper-alloyed hoards were excluded from the study, which is a selection rule of unknown direction. Graeber's wider debt-before-barter thesis is contested; the specific Mesopotamian facts here are not, and Goetzmann is the safer citation for the finance-history framing. **Read more:** Goetzmann, *Money Changes Everything* (2016).] The fourth question was about Europe, and this is the answer that has changed most. The old line was that Bronze Age Europe sat outside the world system whose cores were in West Asia and the Indian Ocean. That is not right, and the thing that changed it is tin. The obstacle had never been the artefacts but the absence of a reference base: nobody had characterised the ores, so there was nothing to compare an ingot against. A Durham-led programme built one, and the discrimination runs in two steps.

Cornish and Devon cassiterites carry up to 176 parts per million of indium where Iberian and French ores are under ten, and indium survives smelting, which is what makes it readable on an ingot rather than on a rock; that removes Iberia and France. Lead-isotope model age then separates the two survivors, the Erzgebirge coming out at 318 to 323 million years against Cornwall and Devon at 274 to 293, and tin from three radiocarbon-dated Israeli wrecks gives 290. One sentence keeps that honest in a seminar: tin isotopes alone cannot do this job, because the tin provinces overlap too much, and the work is done by indium and by lead-isotope model age. What is settled is the Cornish case for those wrecks. What is not settled is Uluburun, where two laboratories read the same cargo and reach incompatible answers, one programme putting the ingots inside Cornish and Devon ranges and another attributing roughly two-thirds to the Taurus and a third to Central Asia, three thousand kilometres east. Concede the strongest point against the Cornish reading rather than smoothing it: the Uluburun ingots measure 2 to 7 parts per million of indium against up to 176 in Cornish ore, and indium is the discriminator. The verdict here rests on the Israeli wrecks.^[**Sources:** Williams et al. (2025) for the Durham ore programme, the indium discrimination and the model ages; Powell et al. (2022) for the Taurus and Musiston attribution of 105 Uluburun ingots; Berger et al. (2023) for the indium measurements that cut against the Cornish reading of that cargo. **Worth knowing:** Berger is a co-author on two of the three, so the lines of evidence are less independent than they look, and lead-isotope provenancing at Uluburun is compromised by lead contamination running from 22 ppm to 11.5 per cent. **Read more:** Williams et al. (2025).]

So the answer is not "peripheral" in the sense students expect. Britain supplied tin, without which there is no bronze, to a network whose demand, capital, weights, writing and organisation all sat in West Asia. That is a resource periphery *inside* the system, which is a different thing from being outside it, and the production model is what makes "periphery" precise rather than dismissive. The tin came from decentralised small alluvial workings, worked part-time alongside farming, handed to coastal trading places and passed down the line. There was no direct contact of any kind between Britain and the Levant: nobody in Cornwall knew where the metal ended up and nobody in Ugarit knew where it started. Britain supplied an input; it did not organise, price or capture the trade in it. Which is this chapter's sharpest instance of N as power, and the pattern recurs at Potosi, at Banda and at every commodity exporter in the twentieth century: the holder of the scarce resource was not the holder of the rents.

The scale needs care. Perhaps 100 to 200 tonnes of tin a year across all of Europe and the Mediterranean in the mid-second millennium BCE --- and say the caveat in the same breath, because the authors call the figure speculative. It is scaled from copper output at three mines on an assumed ten per cent tin-to-copper ratio, then extrapolated across more than a hundred known mines, and a number built by multiplying an uncertain quantity by an assumed coefficient inherits the uncertainty of both. For proportion: Cornwall and Devon produced about 400 tonnes a year in 1200 CE on substantially the same technology with some six thousand mainly part-time workers. A strategic flow, then, and not a large one. None of which makes Europe simple. Varna on the Black Sea, around 4500 BCE, yielded some three thousand gold objects weighing roughly six kilograms, more gold than every other fifth-millennium find in the world put together, and the Durrington pigs above show the same island mobilising animals across most of its length to one place. Organisational sophistication and peripheral position are independent facts, and this period has both. Behind all four questions stood the forces this module tracks: geography came first, with the Himalayan uplift, the monsoon and the great rivers setting the board; climate was the first dynamic driver, its swings bearing on the rise and fall of cores; and technology --- the sail married to monsoon knowledge, the horse, the wheel, bronze --- turned geographic possibility into movement.^[**Sources:** on scale and the production model, Williams et al. (2025); Anthony (Loc 3941) on Varna; Madgwick et al. (2019) on the Durrington catchment. **Read more:** Anthony, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* (2007).]

## Which input was binding?

Every chapter closes its analysis on the second half of the ledger: which of A, K, L and N was the binding constraint? N was binding everywhere, and it bound in two different ways. As a level, there was no tin in Mesopotamia and Uruk hauled its stone eighty kilometres, so a bronze-using city had to be connected to a continent whether it wanted to be or not. As variance, the river under the Indus cities was not short of water so much as unreliable about it. Two kinds of scarcity in one input, and the second is the one most often missed. A moved, and moved slowest, at eight hundred years for the chariot to cross a continent. L was the residual claimant, since a better technique or a windfall of land was captured as more people rather than as higher income per head, which is Malthus written in this book's notation and why the period's thriving is counted in cities and populations. K was real but thin, and finance was sophisticated without being broad: credit crossed a political frontier at Assur and Kanesh centuries before anyone struck a coin, and it was relationship-based, running between known households and named agents, with nothing in this world resembling an impersonal capital market. And control of N is where the economic power sat, with Dilmun taking a cut at a chokepoint without producing anything, Cyprus with its copper and Cornwall with its tin. Britain had the tin; West Asia had the trade.

## The verdict: where was the centre?

The verdict for this period is that there was no single centre, and it is delivered with low confidence by design. What the evidence shows is several loosely linked riverine cores rather than one integrated world economy with a weight that can be located. The Near East, and Uruk above all, was the most central node, a large urban demand pole and the supplier of metals into the long-distance trade. The Indus led the Gulf trade through its mature phase, and it survives as a bright spot in a thin record rather than as a documented centre. Which way that thinness cuts matters. Because the humid tropics destroy organic evidence, what survives from the Indus is a lower bound on its activity rather than an estimate of it, which licenses a claim about direction and nothing about magnitude. What it does not license is treating the sparseness of the record as though it were evidence for the argument, a move this chapter made in an earlier draft and should not make. Egypt and the forming East Asian core sat largely apart from the western-Eurasian system that the evidence actually documents.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 805); Frahm (Page 46). **Read more:** Frahm, *Assyria* (2023).]

The centre-of-gravity question that runs through the rest of the book is therefore not yet applicable. This period neither supports nor contradicts the claim that Asia was central, because it predates a connected system in which a centre of gravity is a meaningful idea. The first chapter at which the question becomes answerable is the next one, when Alexander and the Achaemenid inheritance fuse the channels into something like a single trans-Eurasian system. What this chapter contributes is structural rather than evidential: it lays down the monsoon and the channel geography that will later make the Indian Ocean the natural integrator. Two cautions govern how the period's own thriving should be read. The denominator has to be kept honest, since these were overwhelmingly agrarian subsistence economies in which the great majority farmed and never handled a trade good, and the long-distance traffic described here was a thin and lucrative network laid over that mass rather than the bulk of output. And whatever thriving the period shows was measured in numbers rather than income per head: more food meant more people rather than richer people, the Malthusian condition humanity shared with every other species. The switch from measuring an economy by its scale to measuring it by the living standards of the people in it lies far ahead, at the Great Divergence of [Chapter 7](07-great-divergence.qmd).^[**Sources:** Pearson (Ch.1) on the monsoon deep structure and the channels; Scott (Page 631) on the agrarian denominator. **Read more:** Pearson, *The Indian Ocean* (2003).]

::: {.callout-warning}
## The debate: how much weight should geography carry?
Cunliffe, and Diamond before him, lean hard on geography as the deciding force --- the mountains and monsoon and grass corridors setting what was possible. The counter stresses human agency and contingency, the choices that geography permitted but did not dictate. The climate-collapse story is contested in the same way. The 4.2 ka weakening of the monsoon is invoked behind the Harappan decline, and drought behind the Late Bronze Age Collapse, yet the palaeo-record does not cleanly show a sharp, sustained drought at the right moment, so mono-causal climate accounts overreach. The sensible posture is to hold both at once: deep structures shaped the board on which the period was played, but people still chose the moves. Name the positions, weigh them, and leave the question genuinely open.
:::

**Data exhibit --- the Uluburun cargo, a dataset of one.** With almost no quantitative records, a single well-excavated shipwreck does the work that a price series does in later chapters. The cargo is itemised above, and @fig-uluburun plots the two metals. *What you could do with this:* infer how many separate economies one hull implicates, and ask what the copper-to-tin ratio implies about where the metals were sourced and where the bronze was to be made --- reasoning from one rich object to a whole system, with the uncertainty stated.

## Threads forward

What this chapter hands on is a period fully described rather than a verdict: a world of loosely linked riverine cores, three cycles of integration and collapse, and the first evidence that connection carries shocks as well as goods. That last lesson runs from the Late Bronze Age Collapse through every later disintegration the book meets. The hand-off to the next chapter is geographic and institutional at once. By about 500 BCE the Achaemenid empire had reunited the Near East, iron had loosened the tin bottleneck, and coinage had begun to standardise money. Alexander is where it turns, and the three channels born here would fuse into the first genuinely trans-Eurasian world system --- Rome, Parthia, the Kushans and Han China strung along the routes --- with the monsoon road this chapter laid down as its maritime spine and India at the fulcrum. At that point, for the first time, "where did the weight sit?" becomes a question the evidence can answer.^[**Sources:** Scott (Page 631); Cline (Loc 507) on the fragility lesson. **Citation withdrawn:** the Achaemenid reunification, iron and early coinage claim was attributed to Cline, *1177 B.C.*, but that book does not discuss the Achaemenid reunification and the word "coinage" does not appear in it; the claim needs a source that carries it. Schaps, *The Invention of Coinage and the Monetization of Ancient Greece* (2004), covers the coinage half. **Read more:** Findlay & O'Rourke, *Power and Plenty* (2007).]

## Classic research: the foundations {.unnumbered}

The questions this chapter raises — was Bronze Age trade a market or a redistribution; how much weight should geography carry — descend from a bench of historians, archaeologists and anthropologists.

- **Polanyi (ed., 1957)**, *Trade and Market in the Early Empires* — the substantivist thesis that early "trade" was administered and redistributive rather than market exchange. The reference point for this chapter's central debate; the recent cliometric work below is the market-side rebuttal. Pair them.
- **Algaze (1993; 2008)**, *The Uruk World System* and *Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization* — the "Uruk world system" and the early peak-and-contraction that predates the Gulf trade.
- **Adams (1981)**, *Heartland of Cities* — the classic survey-archaeology of Mesopotamian urbanisation and settlement.
- **Sherratt (1981)**, "Plough and Pastoralism: Aspects of the Secondary Products Revolution," in *Pattern of the Past* — the traction/wool/dairy thesis; teach as contested (discrete event vs gradual adoption).
- **Possehl (2002)**, *The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective* — the standard synthesis and the "transformation, not collapse" reading of the Harappan decline.
- **Anthony (2007)**, *The Horse, the Wheel, and Language* — horse domestication, the Sintashta chariot, and the Indo-European expansions; the steppe-as-engine story.
- **Cline (2014)**, *1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed* — the systemic-fragility reading of the Late Bronze Age Collapse; this chapter's first "integration creates fragility" case.
- **Graeber (2011)**, *Debt: The First 5,000 Years* — credit, debt and the *amargi* cancellations; the case that finance preceded coinage.

## At the research frontier: recent cliometric work {.unnumbered}

A striking amount of recent economics reaches back into deep prehistory — fitting trade models to cuneiform tablets, and testing the origins of states, farming and the Malthusian regime. Every entry verified.

- **Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019)**, "Trade, Merchants, and the Lost Cities of the Bronze Age," *Quarterly Journal of Economics* 134(3): 1455–1503 — a structural gravity model fit to ~12,000 Old Assyrian merchant tablets from Kanesh that recovers trade costs and even triangulates the locations of lost cities. The chapter's proof that Bronze Age long-distance trade was a genuine, estimable market. [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjz009]
- **Mayshar, Moav & Pascali (2022)**, "The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability?" *Journal of Political Economy* 130(4): 1091–1144 — hierarchy and taxation arose from the *appropriability* of storable cereals, not from higher farm productivity; the institutional micro-foundation under the riverine cores. [DOI 10.1086/718372]
- **Matranga (2024)**, "The Ant and the Grasshopper: Seasonality and the Invention of Agriculture," *Quarterly Journal of Economics* 139(3): 1467–1504 — rising climatic seasonality pushed foragers into storage and sedentism, the precondition for farming and surplus; grounds the chapter's "geography and climate as master force" in recent data. [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjae012]
- **Ashraf & Galor (2011)**, "Dynamics and Stagnation in the Malthusian Epoch," *American Economic Review* 101(5): 2003–2041 — the canonical empirical statement that, before 1800, technology and land raised population density rather than income per head. The frontier anchor for this chapter's quantity-vs-quality yardstick, and the thread it hands to [Chapter 7](07-great-divergence.qmd). [DOI 10.1257/aer.101.5.2003]

::: {.callout-note}
## Research in focus — Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu (2019): a gravity model on cuneiform
- **Aim** — to show that Bronze Age long-distance trade obeyed the same economic regularities as modern trade, and to use them to locate cities now lost.
- **Question** — can a structural gravity model, fit to ancient merchant records, recover trade costs and even the geographic position of unknown trading posts?
- **Data & method** — roughly 12,000 clay tablets from the Old Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh (early second millennium BCE), recording shipments between named cities; a structural gravity model in which trade falls with distance is fit to the recorded flows, and the locations of lost cities are estimated as the coordinates that best rationalise the trade pattern.
- **Findings** — trade fell with distance just as the modern gravity equation predicts; the model recovers sensible trade costs and places several lost cities close to where independent historical guesses had put them, with a few testable new predictions.
- **Caveats** — the data are one merchant network in one region and period, heavily weighted to tin and textiles; the gravity structure is imposed, not proven, and the city-location estimates are probabilistic.

*Sources: Barjamovic, Chaney, Coşar & Hortaçsu, "Trade, Merchants, and the Lost Cities of the Bronze Age," Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(3), 2019 [DOI 10.1093/qje/qjz009].*
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Research in focus — Ashraf & Galor (2011): the Malthusian regime, and why "success" meant numbers
- **Aim** — to test the central prediction of the Malthusian model for the pre-industrial world: that productivity gains raised population, not living standards.
- **Question** — across the long pre-1800 era, did better technology and land translate into higher income per head, or simply into more people?
- **Data & method** — assembled cross-country data on population density and income for the pre-industrial period and related them to measures of technological and land productivity, testing the Malthusian mechanism.
- **Findings** — places with better technology and more productive land supported denser populations but not higher income per head; prosperity was converted into numbers, exactly as Malthus predicted, until the regime broke around 1800.
- **Caveats** — deep-history income and population figures are reconstructions with wide error bands; the result characterises the regime on average, not every local episode.

*Sources: Ashraf & Galor, "Dynamics and Stagnation in the Malthusian Epoch," American Economic Review 101(5), 2011 [DOI 10.1257/aer.101.5.2003]. The quantity-vs-quality distinction it formalises is the yardstick paid off at [Chapter 7](07-great-divergence.qmd).*
:::

### Questions for consideration {.unnumbered}

*Essay / exam style — reward the four-questions toolkit and the live debate, not recall.*

1. *"Before prices, how can we know a 'world economy' existed?"* Answer with Bronze Age evidence — the diffusion of goods, shared standards, and the direction of the ships.
2. *"Integration creates fragility."* Assess this claim using the Late Bronze Age Collapse and the contraction of the Uruk world system.
3. The Harappans ran the Gulf trade, yet the Indus survives as "a bright spot in a thin record." Explain how that thinness can *support* rather than undermine the claim that the record under-documents the East.
4. How much explanatory weight should climate carry in the end of the Harappan urban phase? Distinguish abrupt-forcing, gradual-hydrological, and multi-causal accounts.
5. *"Was Bronze Age trade a market, or redistribution?"* Use Mesopotamia (Polanyi) and the Kanesh tablet evidence (Barjamovic et al.) to frame both sides.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Cross-cutting questions (collected at the end of the book)
The book closes with a bank of questions spanning several chapters. Those this chapter opens:
- **Quantity vs quality.** This chapter introduces the distinction between aggregate ("more people") and per-capita ("richer people") success. Trace it through [Chapter 3](03-maritime-apogee.qmd), [Chapter 4](04-high-medieval-mongol.qmd) and [Chapter 7](07-great-divergence.qmd): when is a big economy legitimately a *rich* one?
- **Measuring integration.** Compare measuring integration by the diffusion of goods (this chapter) with measuring it by price convergence ([Chapter 8](08-first-global-economy.qmd)): what does each method see that the other misses?
:::

```{r}
#| label: ch-01-exercise
#| eval: false
# The Uluburun wreck as a dataset of one, and population as a prosperity proxy.

#    estimated; ~175 glass ingots; >=149 Canaanite jars holding ~1 t terebinth resin;
#    135 Cypriot vessels; ebony, ivory, Baltic amber, Mesopotamian bitumen; products of
#    at least nine or ten cultures). How many economies does one hull imply?
# 1b. The 135 Cypriot vessels aboard are twice the number known from the whole Aegean for
#    the entire Late Bronze Age (Pulak 1998: 204). If one wreck doubles the record, what
#    does the surviving record measure - trade, or the accidents of preservation?
# 2. What does the ~10:1 copper:tin ratio say about the intended bronze recipe?
# 3. Load a long-run population series (HYDE 3.3 or Our World in Data) for one region.
# 4. Discuss why "more people" did NOT mean "richer people" — the quantity-vs-quality
#    yardstick — and state the uncertainty in deep-history population estimates.
```
